desc:
A town has n junctions numbered 0 to n - 1 and a set of one-way streets. Each entry edges[i] = [u, v] is a street that can only be driven from junction u to junction v.

Return true if for every ordered pair of junctions (a, b) it is possible to drive from a to b, and false otherwise.

n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,0],[1,3]]  -> true
n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]]              -> false  (no street leads back to junction 0)
n = 1, edges = []                               -> true
constraints: 0 ≤ u, v < n and u ≠ v
No ordered pair [u, v] is listed twice
hints: Running a search from every junction would work but costs n searches. Can you get away with far fewer?
If junction 0 can reach everybody and everybody can reach junction 0, then any a can reach any b by driving through 0.
Run one search from 0 following the streets as given, and a second search from 0 on the graph with every street reversed. Both searches must visit all n junctions.
editorial: Pick any junction as a hub, say 0. The network is strongly connected exactly when 0 can reach every junction and every junction can reach 0. If both hold, a trip from a to b is a trip from a to 0 followed by a trip from 0 to b. If one fails, some pair is clearly disconnected, so the answer is false.

The first condition is an ordinary DFS or BFS from 0. The second is the same search on the reversed graph (every edge u -> v turned into v -> u), because a path from a to 0 in the original graph is a path from 0 to a in the reversed one.
Two linear searches give O(n + m) time. Searching from every junction would be O(n (n + m)). This hub trick is also the first step of Kosaraju's algorithm for strongly connected components.
